If the argument here is that the Catholic theory of the universe is best by being the most perfect, it is necessary to clearly lay out exactly what the Catholic theory is (while further describing the failures of other theories). Though of course, with two thousand years of theologians, councils, encyclicals, and catechesis, this simply cannot be fully done here. However, important and relevant points of doctrine can be introduced.

Enough was said for our purposes of Christianity and the importance of the Son and the Trinity in Treatise 5, including discussion of the Magisterium and the history of the Church. We can point out briefly that the Church consists of three aspects (following the Trinitarian model that we observe all throughout the universe): it is Scripture, Tradition, and the Magisterium. We have discussed the Magisterium as partial revelation through the Spirit becoming more perfect over time, and most people understand that Scripture is held to be divinely inspired text (which logically could only have been canonized through something such as the Magisterium—the Old Testament itself was never fully canonized until the coming of Christ; prior to Christ all Jews agreed on the five books of the Torah, but concerning all else there were arguments about what was and was not inspired text). The Tradition is the apostolic succession of the Church and the memory it has of all the councils and discussions and the works of its theologians, and consists in large part of powerful rational arguments for all the doctrines that the Church holds, but it also consists of the oral teachings of the Apostles themselves, which they have passed down from the time of Christ. These teachings often or always overlap with what is taught in Scripture (and, as has been stated before, predated the New Testament; see 1 Corinthians 11:2 and Acts 2:42).

When discussing Catholicism it is also critically important to discuss Natural Law, the contemplation of which began truly with Aristotle and was thoroughly refined by Doctors of the Church, particularly St. Thomas Aquinas. And no, a pre-Christian origin does not contradict the thoroughly Christian nature of the Natural Law, for remember that the Logos, the immaterial order of the universe that enables reasoning and mathematical truth and morality and the like, is Christ, is God, and has existed from the very beginning[22].

We have mentioned the second tenet of the Natural Law already, but it is time to list all three (of course there are three) tenets together (and note that we are discussing Natural Law in the classical sense, and so we are speaking theologically, and not "naturalistically" or materially):

  • Human nature is moral (free)
  • Nature is intelligible (meaningful)
  • Nature is teleological (purpose-driven)[23]

We have shown that Enlightenment thinkers (materialists) are forced to reject the second tenet because they reject the immaterial and therefore reject meaning and the ideal. It turns out that Protestantism, through its doctrine of Sola Scriptura, can in its more extreme forms such as Calvinism or even Lutherism, lend itself to this same rejection of the second tenet; if only the Bible is intelligible, then nature is not, and all knowledge of God and therefore the universe itself must come from the Bible alone—i.e. nothing can be learned from reason.
